name: GetUserSPNs.py - Kerberoast Across Forest Trust
description: Performs Kerberoasting against a foreign forest domain using credentials from the local forest. When a bidirectional trust exists, the foreign DC will issue TGS tickets for service accounts in the foreign domain — encrypted with the foreign service account's hash. Allows cracking foreign forest service account passwords without any credentials in that forest.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY CROSS-FOREST KERBEROASTING WORKS ===
When a bidirectional forest trust exists between INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL and
FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL:
  - Your INLANEFREIGHT credentials are trusted by FREIGHTLOGISTICS
  - You can request Kerberos service tickets FOR services IN FREIGHTLOGISTICS
  - The TGS is encrypted with the FREIGHTLOGISTICS service account's hash
  - Crack offline — same as regular kerberoasting, no credential needed in foreign forest

=== THE -target-domain FLAG ===
This tells GetUserSPNs.py to:
  1. Authenticate TO your domain (INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL) with provided creds
  2. Request a cross-realm TGS for the FOREIGN domain's SPNs
  3. Return hashes encrypted with the foreign account's key

=== OUTPUT ===
$krb5tgs$23$*<spn>*<realm>*... → same format as regular kerberoasting
Crack with: hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

=== FOREIGN USER IN LOCAL GROUP ===
Also check: Get-DomainForeignGroupMember -Domain FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL
If FREIGHTLOGISTICS users are members of INLANEFREIGHT groups (or vice versa),
those accounts may have rights in both domains — high value targets.

=== FIND TRUSTS FIRST ===
Get-DomainTrust → identify bidirectional forest trust
Get-DomainTrust → 'TrustDirection: Bidirectional' = cross-forest kerberoast possible

=== AFTER CRACKING ===
Foreign service account cred → test against foreign DC (Evil-WinRM, CME)
Foreign admin account → DCSync foreign forest if privileged

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

defense.why_it_works: Bidirectional forest trusts allow any authenticated user in the local forest to request Kerberos service tickets for SPNs registered in the foreign forest. The foreign DC issues a TGS encrypted with the target service account's hash — identical mechanics to in-domain Kerberoasting. No credentials in the foreign forest are required; the local forest TGT is accepted via the trust referral chain.
defense.prerequisites: Bidirectional or outbound forest trust from local to target forest. Valid credentials in the local forest (any domain user). SPN-bearing service accounts existing in the foreign forest that have weak, crackable passwords.
defense.impact: Offline cracking of foreign forest service account hashes. Compromised credentials may provide privileged access in the foreign forest — especially if the SPN account is a service/admin account with cross-domain group membership or local admin rights.
defense.detection: Windows Security Event 4769 on the foreign forest's DCs showing TGS requests from a foreign-forest account (anomalous — normal cross-forest Kerberos is machine-to-machine). Multiple TGS requests for different SPNs in rapid succession from a single source is a Kerberoasting indicator. The requesting account's domain will differ from the DC's domain — a detectable anomaly in the foreign forest's logs.
defense.prevention: Set forest trust to Selective Authentication (limits which users can authenticate across the trust — prevents arbitrary domain users from requesting tickets). Enforce AES-only Kerberos on service accounts (RC4 disabled) to make cracking infeasible. Audit SPN accounts in the foreign forest and ensure they have long random passwords (25+ chars). Regularly review bidirectional forest trust necessity.
defense.evasion: Request TGS for one SPN at a time with delays to avoid burst patterns. Target only RC4-enabled accounts. -request flag requests only tickets — no spray noise. Blend timing with normal cross-forest authentication activity.
defense.misconfiguration: Domain trusts (especially bidirectional and forest trusts) extend authentication boundaries. SID filtering is often disabled on forest trusts to support legacy applications — but this allows an attacker with Domain Admin in a child domain to forge a golden ticket with ExtraSids claiming Domain Admin SID in the parent/trusted forest. Without SID filtering (SIDHistory filtering), domain boundaries offer no security isolation.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Bidirectional forest trust without SID filtering:
Get-ADTrust -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Direction, SIDFilteringQuarantined
# SIDFilteringQuarantined: False  <-- SID filtering DISABLED
# Direction: BiDirectional        <-- both domains trust each other

# Child domain to parent: SID filtering is always disabled by default
# Enterprise Admin SID (S-1-5-21-<root>-519) can be added to ExtraSids
# Golden ticket with ExtraSids = cross-domain privilege escalation
defense.secure_config:
# Enable SID filtering on external/forest trusts:
netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine:yes
# 'Quarantine' = SID filtering enabled — ExtraSids from other domain are stripped

# For child-to-parent trusts (SID filtering can't be enabled without breaking functionality):
# Use Selective Authentication instead of full trust
# Only accounts explicitly granted 'Allowed to Authenticate' can use the trust
netdom trust <ParentDomain> /domain:<ChildDomain> /SelectiveAuth:yes

# Restrict SIDHistory (prevents ExtraSids abuse):
# Audit accounts with SIDHistory:
Get-ADUser -Filter {SIDHistory -like '*'} -Properties SIDHistory

# Monitor cross-forest authentication:
# Event 4769 on parent DC with ticket from child domain user
